title: Playing with what I know
keyIdea: In pretend play a young child uses what they already know from real life. They act out things they have seen, in the right order (get the pan, put in the food, stir, serve), they let one thing stand for another (a block is a phone), and they copy the words and jobs of real people such as a doctor, a cook or a shop helper. Pretending is not a mistake: the child knows the block is a block. It is early thinking with symbols.

kid: You see lots of things at home. You see cooking, washing and shopping. In pretend play, you play them too!
A block can be a phone. A box can be a car. A stick can be a spoon. You know it is a block. You just pretend.
Pretend soup goes in order, like real soup. Get the pan. Put in a carrot. Stir it. Pour it in a bowl.
You can be a doctor and say “Open wide.” You can be the shop helper and say “That is 2 coins, please.”
adult: This is symbolic play, also called pretend play. Most children start to pretend between 12 and 24 months, and it grows fast at 2 to 3. In England, the EYFS guidance Development Matters (2021) lists it under Expressive Arts and Design. For birth to three it says children start to develop pretend play, pretending that one object represents another, like a block held to the ear as a phone. At 3 and 4 they use an object to represent something else even when the two are not alike. In the US, the Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework covers it under Approaches to Learning: creativity.

Three skills sit underneath. Object substitution is letting one thing stand for another, like a box for a car. Piaget saw it as the start of the symbolic function: holding an idea in mind that is not there. Deferred imitation is copying an action seen earlier, like stirring a pot the way you do. Scripts are the steps of a familiar event, such as cooking or a trip to the doctor, in order. Children play them in order because they have stored the routine. Role play then adds the words and jobs of real people.

Common mistakes to watch for: thinking a child who calls a banana a phone is confused (they know it is a banana, so ask who is calling); stopping pretend play because it looks silly or messy; thinking pretend needs real-looking toys, when boxes, blocks and cloth often spark more ideas; correcting copying as doing it wrong, when copying is how they learn the routine; and taking over the story instead of following their lead. A big review by Lillard and others (2013) found pretend play goes along with language and social growth. It is one good route, not a magic one.

In the lab your child cooks pretend soup in the right order and turns a block, a box and a stick into a phone, a car and a spoon. They put real things into the doctor, kitchen and shop corners, match what people say to who says it, and turn one big box into a car, a bed and a house. Every step works by dragging or by tapping big buttons. Read the Challenge aloud together.

familyTip: Put out a box, a wooden spoon and a cloth and wait. If your child picks something up and pretends, join their game, not your own: “Ooh, is that a phone? Who is calling?” Then add one real-life step they know, like “Shall we cook dinner first, then eat?”

visual.caption: Doctor play or shop play? Drag each thing, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: cook pretend soup in order, make a block a phone, sort play things, match what people say and turn one box into lots of things.

practice.prompt: Mia holds a block to her ear and says “Hello!” What is she doing?
choices: Pretending the block is a phone
practice.hint: Does Mia know it is a block? She is using it as something else.
practice.explain: She is pretending. One thing stands for another. That is clever thinking, not a mix-up.

practice.prompt: You have {n} blocks. Each block is a pretend phone. How many pretend phones?
practice.hint: Each block is one pretend phone. Count the blocks.
practice.explain: {n} blocks make {n} pretend phones. One block, one phone.

practice.prompt: A pretend game has {s} steps. You did {n} steps. How many steps are left?
practice.hint: Start at {s} steps and take away the {n} you did.
practice.explain: {s} steps take away {n} done leaves {=s-n} steps.

practice.prompt: What do we do first to make pretend soup?
practice.hint: What do we need before we can cook?
practice.explain: The soup cooks in the pan, so we get the pan first. We play it in the order we see at home.

pool.prompt: Who says “Open wide and say ahh”?
pool.explain: A doctor looks in your mouth. In pretend play we copy the words real people say.

pool.prompt: Can a box be a car in pretend play?
choices: No, it is only a box
Only if it has real wheels
pool.hint: In pretend play, can one thing be something else?
pool.explain: Yes. In pretend play a box can be a car, a bed or a house. We know it is a box, and we pretend.

pool.prompt: Where do coins go in pretend play?
pool.hint: Where do we pay for things?
pool.explain: We pay with coins at the shop, so coins go in the shop play.

pool.prompt: Ben stirs a pretend pot, just like Dad does. What is Ben doing?
pool.hint: Where did Ben see stirring before?
pool.explain: Ben is copying what he saw Dad do. Copying is how little ones learn how things go.

pool.prompt: Which thing can be a pretend spoon?
pool.hint: Which one can you hold and stir with?
pool.explain: A stick is long like a spoon, so we can stir with it and pretend.

pool.prompt: {a} children play shop and {b} children play doctor. How many children are playing pretend?
pool.hint: Count the shop children, then count on the doctor children.
pool.explain: {a} and {b} more make {=a+b} children playing pretend.

pool.prompt: What does a plaster go with in pretend play?
pool.hint: Who helps when you hurt your knee?
pool.explain: A plaster helps a hurt knee, so it goes with doctor play.

pool.hint: We cook it first. What do we do when it is ready?
pool.explain: We pour the soup in a bowl last, when it is cooked. Then we eat it.

pool.prompt: You give each of {n} teddies a pretend cup. How many cups do you need?
pool.hint: One cup for each teddy. Count the teddies.
pool.explain: {n} teddies get one cup each, so you need {n} pretend cups.
